strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: generating navigable, immersive 3D urban scenes purely from satellite imagery, without requiring costly 3D scans or ground-level data, which has clear applications in simulation, gaming, and robotics.

The two-stage pipeline (satellite-based 3DGS reconstruction with appearance modeling/regularization, followed by curriculum-based iterative dataset update with diffusion-based render refinement) is a sensible and reasonably novel combination of existing techniques (3DGS, WildGaussians-style appearance embeddings, FlowEdit/prompt-to-prompt editing, IDU-style refinement) tailored specifically to the satellite-to-ground-view domain.

The curriculum strategy (progressively lowering camera elevation across episodes) is a clean and intuitively justified design choice, directly motivated by the empirically observed degradation of 3DGS quality at lower elevation angles (Fig. 4), and is validated in ablations.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation: two datasets (DFC2019 satellite imagery and GoogleEarth), comparisons against both satellite-reconstruction baselines (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, Mip-Splatting, CoR-GS) and city-generation baselines (CityDreamer, GaussianCity), quantitative distribution-based and pixel-aligned metrics, qualitative comparisons, ablations for each design component, a user study with 89 participants, rendering efficiency benchmarks, and extensive supplementary results across additional AOIs.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, architecture and prompt details in the appendix, dataset/AOI specification tables, and a stated plan to release code and (partial) data.
The paper is transparent about limitations (compute cost, over-smoothing at extreme street-level views) and includes an ethics statement and explicit LLM usage disclosure.
weaknesses: The core methodological components (3DGS, appearance embeddings from WildGaussians, opacity regularization, monocular depth supervision via Pearson correlation, FlowEdit/prompt-to-prompt refinement, iterative dataset update as in Instruct-NeRF2NeRF/IM-3D) are all adopted from prior work; the primary novelty is their combination and the curriculum ordering of elevation angles, which is a comparatively incremental contribution.

Evaluation is entirely reference-free/proxy-based: because no ground-truth 3D or street-level geometry exists for these scenes, quality is assessed against Google Earth Studio renders (which are themselves synthetic/game-engine-like reconstructions) using distribution metrics (FID, CMMD) and a subjective user study; there is no way to verify true geometric accuracy or faithfulness to the real world, which is a significant evidentiary gap for a paper claiming 'geometrically accurate' reconstruction.

Pixel-aligned metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) are reported as "secondary" and are frequently won by baselines (e.g., CoR-GS attains best SSIM/LPIPS in several DFC2019 scenes in Table 8), suggesting the proposed method may sacrifice pixel fidelity for perceptual/distributional plausibility—this trade-off deserves more explicit discussion rather than being downplayed.

The synthesis stage relies on hallucination from a generic diffusion prior (FLUX.1) to fill occluded facades and lower-elevation views; while visually plausible, this raises the risk of generating architecturally incorrect or fabricated structural details not present in the true environment, which is important for applications (e.g., robotics/simulation) that may need factual geometric grounding—the paper does not quantify hallucination error against any independent geometric ground truth.

Baseline comparisons may be somewhat uneven: city-generation baselines (CityDreamer, GaussianCity) are trained on much smaller-scale, domain-specific datasets with different input modalities (semantic maps/height fields) and are evaluated out-of-domain, and several other relevant satellite-NVS methods are excluded due to lack of released code (acknowledged by the authors), leaving open the possibility that some comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples.

The computational cost of the synthesis stage (~6 hours per scene on an A6000, plus reconstruction time) somewhat undercuts the 'scalable city creation' framing, and scaling behavior to genuinely large, multi-block or full-city extents is not demonstrated (experiments are on modest per-AOI patches).

Ablation studies are conducted only on a single AOI (JAX_068), limiting confidence that the reported component-wise gains generalize across the diverse urban environments the paper otherwise emphasizes.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and relatively underexplored problem: building immersive, free-flight navigable city-scale 3D scenes purely from satellite imagery, without relying on street-level data, semantic maps, or height fields that prior city-generation works require.

The two-stage pipeline (3DGS reconstruction with appearance/opacity/pseudo-depth regularization, followed by curriculum-based iterative dataset update with diffusion-based render refinement) is a sensible engineering synthesis of known techniques tailored to the specific failure modes of satellite-only reconstruction (low parallax, occluded facades, multi-date illumination variance).

Reasonably thorough empirical protocol: two datasets (DFC2019, GoogleEarth), comparisons against both satellite-reconstruction baselines (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, Mip-Splatting+appearance, CoR-GS) and city-generation baselines (CityDreamer, GaussianCity), a user study with 89 participants, and ablations isolating each proposed component (appearance modeling, opacity regularization, depth supervision, multi-sample diffusion, curriculum ordering).

Good engineering details and disclosure (prompt specifications, curriculum schedules, FlowEdit parameters, pseudo-camera sampling) in the appendix that aid reproducibility, along with an explicit LLM-usage disclosure.
Rendering efficiency results (real-time on modest hardware) are a useful practical contribution if the quality claims hold up.
weaknesses: No evaluation against true 3D geometric ground truth (e.g., DSM/point-cloud from DFC2019, which does include reference 3D data) is performed, despite repeated claims of 'geometric accuracy' and '3D-justified geometry'; all quantitative evidence relies on 2D perceptual similarity (FID_CLIP, CMMD, PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) to Google Earth Studio renders, which are themselves a different, imperfect proxy for ground truth rather than verified geometry, and may share stylistic bias with the diffusion-refined outputs’ target domain (clean, well-lit urban imagery) rather than reflecting true scene fidelity.

The core technical novelty is modest: most individual components (WildGaussians-style appearance embeddings, entropy-based opacity regularization, MoGe-based pseudo-depth supervision, FlowEdit/prompt-to-prompt refinement, iterative dataset update à la Instruct-NeRF2NeRF) are directly adopted from prior work; the main contribution is the curriculum-based ordering of viewpoints and their combination for this task, which is a comparatively incremental algorithmic insight.

Because the method hallucinates occluded facades and fine geometric/texture detail using an open-domain diffusion prior, the resulting 3D structures are not guaranteed to correspond to real-world geometry — this directly conflicts with claims of 'geometrically accurate' reconstruction and could be problematic for applications (robotics, simulation, urban planning) that need faithful geometry rather than plausible-looking hallucination; this tension is only briefly acknowledged in the limitations.

Baseline comparisons may be unequal in a way that is not fully controlled for: city-generation baselines (CityDreamer, GaussianCity) are designed to take semantic maps/height fields as input and are evaluated here under different (arguably disadvantageous) conditions, while reconstruction baselines are not retrained with the same supervision signals (depth, appearance embeddings) as the proposed method — making it hard to isolate whether gains come from the proposed algorithmic ideas or from additional supervision/engineering not given to baselines.
Ablation studies are conducted on a single AOI (JAX_068) only, which limits confidence that the reported component-wise gains generalize across the diverse scenes used in the main comparison.

The user study methodology is coarse (single forced-choice winner per video, no statistical significance testing reported, unclear randomization/blinding details) and the 'winrate' presentation (e.g., 97/97/97 vs 3/3/3) suggests near-unanimous but possibly biased preference given the researchers' own method being visually the most 'polished' due to diffusion refinement, independent of actual geometric correctness.

The method requires substantial per-scene compute (~1h reconstruction + ~6h synthesis on an A6000) and hand-tuned prompts, which is in tension with the framing as a readily scalable alternative to costly 3D reconstruction, and this cost is only briefly mentioned as a limitation.

Minor clarity/consistency issues: the claim that pixel-aligned metrics are 'meaningful' only for the GoogleEarth dataset is contradicted by Table 1 nonetheless reporting PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS for DFC2019 under non-paired-camera conditions, muddying interpretation of those numbers.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: creating immersive, explorable 3D urban scenes purely from satellite imagery without costly 3D ground-truth annotations or domain-specific training data.

The two-stage pipeline (3DGS reconstruction with appearance modeling/opacity/depth regularization, followed by curriculum-based iterative dataset update with diffusion refinement) is a sensible and reasonably novel combination of existing building blocks tailored specifically to the satellite-to-ground-view domain, e.g. the curriculum-based descent from sky to ground view angles is a nice insight motivated by clear empirical observation (Figure 4).

Extensive quantitative results on two datasets (DFC2019 and GoogleEarth) against both satellite-reconstruction baselines (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, Mip-Splatting, CoR-GS) and city-generation baselines (CityDreamer, GaussianCity), consistently showing improvements across distribution-based and pixel-level metrics.

Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contribution of appearance modeling, opacity regularization, depth supervision, multiple diffusion samples, and curriculum learning, each showing clear incremental benefit.
User studies with a sizeable number of participants (89) corroborate the quantitative findings with large reported win-rates.
Good engineering results: real-time rendering (11 FPS on modest hardware, 40 FPS on a MacBook Air), which is practically relevant for the stated application of immersive exploration.
Reasonably transparent reporting of implementation details, hyperparameters, and limitations, plus a reproducibility statement and disclosed intent to release code/data.
weaknesses: The evaluation is largely against Google Earth Studio (GES) renders treated as pseudo ground truth, but GES itself is a rendered reconstruction (not verified real-world ground truth), which raises concerns about circularity, especially since the distribution metrics (FID, CMMD) mainly assess perceptual/stylistic similarity to GES rather than true geometric fidelity of the recovered urban structure.

Aside from the subjective user-study "geometric accuracy" question, there is no quantitative 3D geometric evaluation (e.g., depth error, mesh/point-cloud comparison to LiDAR or photogrammetric ground truth) to substantiate claims of improved geometric accuracy, which is a core claimed contribution.

Several closely related satellite-view synthesis and sparse-view diffusion-based reconstruction methods are excluded from comparison because code/models are unavailable (footnote lists many), which somewhat weakens the completeness of the empirical comparison, though this is a reasonable practical constraint.

The diffusion-based refinement (FlowEdit/FLUX) can hallucinate facade and structural details not actually present in the satellite input; the paper does not quantify how often generated content deviates from plausible/real structure versus merely being visually pleasing, which is an important risk for applications requiring geometric fidelity (e.g., robotics/simulation as claimed in the intro).

The method is computationally heavy (~6 hours per scene for the synthesis stage on an A6000), and scaling to true city-scale (beyond block-scale AOIs) is left as future work, so the "large-scale" framing in the abstract/intro is somewhat aspirational relative to the block-scale scenes actually demonstrated.

Some technical novelty is incremental: the individual components (WildGaussians-style appearance modeling, opacity regularization, IDU with diffusion refinement, prompt-to-prompt/FlowEdit editing) are adapted from prior works; the primary novelty is the specific combination and curriculum scheduling for the satellite domain, which is a reasonable but modest algorithmic contribution.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important gap: creating immersive, navigable 3D urban scenes purely from multi-view satellite imagery without relying on costly 3D scans or street-level data, which is valuable for gaming, simulation, and robotics applications.

The proposed curriculum-based Iterative Dataset Update (IDU) strategy is well-motivated by an explicit empirical observation (Fig. 4: quality degradation at lower elevation angles) and is a sensible adaptation of prior IDU/InstructNeRF2NeRF-style pipelines to the specific failure modes of satellite-based reconstruction (occluded facades, limited parallax).

Extensive and fairly systematic experimental evaluation: two datasets (DFC2019 and GoogleEarth) with multiple AOIs, comparisons against both satellite-reconstruction baselines (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, CoR-GS, Mip-Splatting) and city-generation baselines (CityDreamer, GaussianCity), quantitative metrics (FID_CLIP, CMMD, PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), and two independent user studies with 44 participants each.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component (appearance modeling, opacity regularization, pseudo-camera depth supervision, multi-sample diffusion averaging, curriculum vs. random view sampling, SDEdit vs. FlowEdit) with both quantitative tables and qualitative failure visualizations.

Good engineering detail and reproducibility effort: extensive supplementary material specifying hyperparameters, prompts, camera sampling strategies, runtime/memory profiling, and additional robustness checks (prompt sensitivity, random-seed diversity, transient-object handling, multi-block scalability, generalization to complex/non-Manhattan geometries like castles and cathedrals).
Clear identification of limitations (fixed heuristic camera trajectory, requirement for off-nadir imagery) rather than overselling the method.
weaknesses: The evaluation ground truth is itself synthetic: Google Earth Studio (GES) renders are used as pseudo-ground-truth for both datasets, including DFC2019, where the paper itself admits systematic illumination/color gaps between real WorldView-3 imagery and GES references make pixel-level scores unreliable; this raises concerns about whether the reported perceptual/distributional metrics actually reflect real-world photorealism versus similarity to another synthetic renderer.

No comparison against real ground-level photographs or independent geometric ground truth (e.g., LiDAR-based quantitative accuracy is only mentioned qualitatively/in an ablation context on one AOI, not systematically reported against baselines), which weakens claims of "geometrically accurate" reconstruction.

The diffusion-based refinement can hallucinate content not grounded in the actual satellite observations (e.g., Fig. 23 shows arbitrary invented storefront signage text differing across random seeds), which is a meaningful concern for a system whose stated goal is faithful reconstruction of real urban scenes for navigation/simulation, not free-form generation; the paper does not deeply discuss the risk/implications of such hallucinated fine details.

Several recently published, closely related baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., SkySplat, MagicCity, Sat2RealCity, Horizon-GS) are excluded from comparison due to unavailable code, leaving open how the method compares to the most relevant recent competitors despite them being discussed as directly relevant prior art.

Computational cost is substantial (up to ~9 hours and ~46GB peak memory for a ~1km×512m two-tile scene on a 48GB A6000), and the demonstrated "multi-block scalability" is limited to merging just two adjacent tiles, which does not strongly substantiate claims of scalability to full city-scale scenes.

The method depends on a fixed heuristic orbital curriculum and look-at grid, which the authors acknowledge can leave blind spots in complex urban geometries at street level; robustness across highly irregular dense/informal urban layouts beyond the tested AOIs is not demonstrated.

The user studies, while informative, lack reported statistical significance testing and rely on forced-choice comparisons among a limited set of baselines and 4 scenes per study, limiting the strength of the human-preference claims.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and under-explored problem: building immersive, freely-navigable 3D urban scenes purely from multi-view satellite imagery, without street-level data or domain-specific 3D training, which has clear applications in simulation, gaming and robotics.

The pipeline is a coherent engineering integration of appearance modeling (WildGaussians-style embeddings) for multi-date imagery, opacity/entropy regularization, pseudo-camera depth supervision via a monocular depth prior, and a curriculum-scheduled Iterative Dataset Update with a text-to-image diffusion model (FlowEdit) to hallucinate occluded facades -- a sensible combination tailored to the specific failure modes of satellite-only reconstruction (fog/blur/floaters at low elevations).

Fairly extensive empirical validation: two datasets (DFC2019 and GoogleEarth) with several AOIs, comparisons against both satellite-reconstruction baselines (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, CoR-GS, Mip-Splatting) and city-generation baselines (CityDreamer, GaussianCity), ablations isolating each component, two independent user studies with a total of 88 participants, and supplementary robustness studies (prompt sensitivity, multi-block scaling, complex/irregular geometries, transient-object handling, stochastic diversity).
Reasonably detailed implementation and hyperparameter disclosure (loss weights, learning rates, network architecture, FlowEdit noise ranges, camera sampling schedule) that aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is largely incremental/recombinatory: appearance embeddings are adopted from WildGaussians, IDU is from Instruct-NeRF2NeRF/LucidDreamer/WonderWorld, refinement uses off-the-shelf FlowEdit+FLUX.1, and depth supervision uses off-the-shelf MoGe. The main contributions (curriculum view scheduling, multi-sample averaging) are reasonable but modest engineering additions rather than fundamentally new methodology, which somewhat undercuts the strong framing ("novel hybrid framework", "first method").

The primary quantitative evaluation (FID_CLIP, CMMD, and even the pixel-level metrics) is computed against Google Earth Studio (GES) renders as pseudo-ground-truth, which are themselves synthetic renderings from Google's proprietary 3D city models rather than real photographs. This makes the comparison partially circular/domain-biased and the paper itself admits pixel-level metrics on DFC2019 are "unreliable" due to systematic illumination/color gaps -- yet these same metrics are used throughout to claim state-of-the-art performance.

Despite the abstract's claim of "geometrically accurate" scenes, there is essentially no rigorous 3D geometric evaluation against real ground truth compared to baselines; the one LiDAR-based MAE/RMSE evaluation (Table 3) is confined to an internal ablation of reconstruction-stage components, not a comparison with competing methods, and the supplementary "coverage" proxy metric is explicitly acknowledged by the authors as unable to detect true holes. The paper conflates photorealism/perceptual-distributional similarity with genuine geometric correctness.

For heavily occluded/hallucinated regions (e.g., building facades), the diffusion model is effectively inventing content with no verifiable ground truth; the qualitative demonstrations on famous landmarks (Neuschwanstein Castle, Wells Cathedral) are particularly concerning because these structures are very likely memorized by the pretrained FLUX.1 diffusion model from web-scale training data, so the impressive facade synthesis there may not generalize to arbitrary, non-iconic city blocks -- this potential confound is not discussed as a limitation.

The 3D-consistency problem for independent per-view 2D diffusion edits is only heuristically mitigated (averaging Nv=2 samples in the photometric loss) rather than solved; the authors acknowledge this expanded, non-optimal denoising distribution directly causes artifacts (Fig. 9c), which is a fairly fundamental soundness gap for a method whose stated goal is faithful geometric reconstruction.

Reported computational cost is high and scales poorly: ~6h45min and up to 46GB peak memory for a single AOI, and ~9 hours for merging just two adjacent tiles into a ~1km x 512m region -- this raises doubts about the practical scalability implied by claims of "scalable 3D urban virtual scene creation" and city-wide applications.

Several recent, closely related satellite-to-3D/city-generation methods cited in related work (e.g., SkySplat, MagicCity, Sat3DGen, Sat2RealCity, Horizon-GS, CityGS-X) are excluded from quantitative comparison (mostly due to code unavailability), which weakens the strength of the state-of-the-art claims given how crowded this sub-area has become.

User studies (44 participants each) report only win-rate percentages without statistical significance testing or inter-rater agreement, and quantitative tables highlight per-scene "best/second/third" results without variance or significance reporting, limiting the rigor of the comparative claims.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important gap: bridging cheap, widely-available satellite imagery with immersive, ground-navigable 3D city reconstruction, avoiding costly street-level 3D data collection.

The hybrid pipeline (3DGS reconstruction + curriculum-based diffusion refinement via Iterative Dataset Update) is a sensible and reasonably novel systems-level integration; the curriculum motivation (Fig. 4, progressive degradation at lower elevations) is clearly demonstrated and directly informs the design.

Thorough experimental validation: two datasets (DFC2019 satellite imagery and GoogleEarth), comparisons against both satellite-reconstruction baselines (Sat-NeRF, EOGS, CoR-GS, Mip-Splatting) and city-generation baselines (CityDreamer, GaussianCity), plus two independent user studies (44 participants each) showing strong human preference.

Extensive and honest ablations isolating each component (appearance modeling, opacity regularization, pseudo-depth supervision, multi-sample diffusion averaging, curriculum vs. random view scheduling, SDEdit vs. FlowEdit), which credibly support the design choices.

Good supplementary robustness checks: multi-block scalability without stitching artifacts, prompt-sensitivity analysis showing tolerance to prompt wording, transient-object disentanglement via per-image embeddings, generalization to complex non-Manhattan geometries (castles, cathedrals) and thin structures (bridges), and stochastic diversity analysis distinguishing fixed geometry from generated appearance.

Practical efficiency is reported and appears reasonable for the target application (real-time rendering at various hardware tiers), and limitations (fixed heuristic camera trajectory, need for off-nadir views) are honestly disclosed.
weaknesses: Ground truth for evaluation is Google Earth Studio (GES) renders rather than real photographs; since GES itself is a rendered textured mesh, this evaluation proxy may not fully capture real-world photorealism/faithfulness gaps, and this domain-gap caveat is not deeply discussed.

Because pixel-aligned metrics are acknowledged as unreliable for hallucinated/occluded regions, the paper leans heavily on distributional metrics (FID_CLIP, CMMD); the improvement is not universal (e.g., Mip-Splatting wins on GoogleEarth scene 219 and overall LPIPS), and the paper's own explanation of exceptions is somewhat post hoc.

The diffusion refinement (FlowEdit/FLUX) hallucinates facade texture that is only loosely constrained by satellite observations; Fig. 23 itself shows arbitrary variation in fine-grained facade content (e.g., random signage text) across seeds, raising questions about semantic faithfulness for applications (robotics, navigation) that assume real-world accuracy, beyond broad geometric consistency.

Many components (appearance embeddings from WildGaussians, IDU paradigm from Instruct-NeRF2NeRF/RealmDreamer, FlowEdit editing) are adapted from existing techniques; the core contribution is largely an application-specific integration/systems contribution rather than a fundamentally new algorithm, which should be read as an Applied/Systems-type contribution even though not explicitly declared as such.

Scalability evidence is limited to two adjacent AOIs (~1km x 512m) requiring ~9 hours on an A6000 GPU; true city-scale applicability (the paper's stated motivation) remains unverified, and several hyperparameters (e.g., disabling opacity regularization for GoogleEarth, elevation schedules, FlowEdit noise bounds) appear to require manual per-dataset tuning, which may limit out-of-the-box generality.

The method fundamentally requires off-nadir multi-date satellite imagery to recover facades, which is explicitly noted as a limitation and restricts applicability to certain satellite archives/regions.
